title: Passive Anti-Theft System (PATS): Start Permission
introduction: I think of the passive anti-theft system (PATS) as the doorman for starting the car: it checks for a valid programmed key when you request a start. The useful distinction here is between permission to start and what happens once the vehicle is running. This overview explains that boundary; it does not provide key-programming or fault-diagnosis instructions.

edits.text: When you press the START/STOP button, the passive anti-theft system (PATS) must detect a valid programmed key inside the vehicle before it permits starting. Preventing a start without that key is how PATS deters theft.
edits.why: Both the key’s programmed validity and its presence inside the vehicle matter. This describes the anti-theft permission check; detecting the key does not establish that every other condition needed to start has been met.

edits.text: PATS does not disable a vehicle that is already running.
edits.why: I keep this boundary in mind when interpreting a complaint: the starting restriction described here does not explain a shutdown after the vehicle is running.
